doc.title: Glenn Zottola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 7, 2020

title: Port Chester jam sessions and learning standards from his mother
summary: Growing up in Port Chester jamming with older beboppers, and how his mother taught him hundreds of standards by ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I grew up in a place called Port Chester, New York, near Connecticut, and this was in the Yonkers area where Ahmad Jamal lives. And there was a bunch of black guys, older. They were good players, they were beboppers and you know, they weren’t famous or anything. And we’d get together every week and I was only maybe 15, 14 years old. Just to play.
And if they played a tune, let’s say you went to one session and they called “How High the Moon” and you didn’t know it. How did you learn it for next time?
Well I was fortunate. When I was five years old my mom, she played by ear also, she sat me on her knee at the piano and she taught me hundreds of standards without a sheet of music. Hundreds. Okay?
Can you explain how and what she was teaching you? Did you have the trumpet?

Yeah. She would comp the changes and sing, and it’s in my DNA. I learned all those standards without a sheet of music, by ear. And then I would, every time I’d come home from school since I was little, grammar school, we would jam every day. Piano and trumpet. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
And years later if you were playing with like a female vocalist who did all those tunes in different keys? It didn’t matter?

No. I knew them. I knew them. I mean the American Songbook is in my DNA. I never really, I’m just starting to do some of Chick Corea’s music, which is not my thing. My whole life is Rogers & Hart and Irving Berlin and Cole Porter. You know that’s my life, as a lot of jazz players from the era we’re talking about, right? Very few guys wrote their own material then.
